docs.title: chap-test-data
docs.text:
Synthetic datasets for Chap, at any size, and the tools to send them to Chap and check its answers.

  • Generate datasets from 10 to 100,000 org units over any number of years, weekly or monthly, with cases, covariates and climate data. Written as Parquet and GeoParquet, and on request as CSV, GeoJSON and the make-dataset JSON bodies the Modeling App sends today.
  • Know the answer in advance. Each dataset comes with an expected.json: what Chap should answer, including for the files it must reject.
  • Upload and check against a running Chap, directly or through a DHIS2 route, with the Python command line or with plain curl.
  • Compare Parquet uploads with today's JSON uploads, on a fast link or a slow, distant one.

docs.title: In one minute
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/dhis2-chap/chap-test-data && cd chap-test-data
uv sync
./generate-datasets.sh --standard-only        # 16 datasets in datasets/, the same every time
uv run chap-test-data generate my-country --org-units 300 --geometry polygon --format geojson
uv run chap-test-data check                   # needs a running Chap; see Getting started

docs.title: A dataset
docs.text:
Every dataset is a folder of files describing the same data:

File What it holds observations.parquet One row per org unit and period: location, time_period, then one numeric column per value. The dataset settings are in the file's chap.* metadata. locations.parquet GeoParquet: one row per org unit with location, name, parent, level and the geometry. locations.geojson The same locations as GeoJSON (--format geojson). make-dataset.columns.json The same dataset as the JSON body the Modeling App sends today (--format json-columns). expected.json What Chap should answer to a dry run of the Parquet files, and the seed used.

The file format and its metadata keys are described in chap-core's dataset files documentation.

docs.title: About
docs.text: chap-test-data is part of Chap, the Climate and Health modelling platform built around DHIS2. Chap forecasts climate-sensitive diseases such as malaria and dengue from health data reported in DHIS2 and from climate data, and helps countries judge how far those forecasts can be trusted.

docs.title: Why it exists
docs.text:
Chap is moving from datasets sent as JSON and stored one value per database row to datasets sent and stored as Parquet files. Testing that needs data in every size, from a handful of districts to 100,000 org units over ten years, and in every shape Chap must accept, reject in part or refuse. Real DHIS2 data cannot be shared freely and does not come in every size, so this tool generates it: realistic enough to behave like the real thing, with the answer Chap should give known in advance.

It is also how the Parquet upload was measured: how much smaller and faster it is than today's JSON, directly and through DHIS2 routes, on fast and on slow, distant links.

docs.title: Related projects
docs.text: Project What it is chap-core The Chap platform: the API, the database, model runs and evaluation chapkit The toolkit for building Chap models as services; its test data generator sets the value ranges used here Chap documentation The Chap project, its models and how to use the Modeling App

docs.title: Timing the checks
docs.text:
Once Chap stores datasets as files (Phase 2), an upload can be checked straight on the files, without a background worker. time-checks runs those checks on dataset folders, without Chap, and times each one:

  • duplicate rows for one org unit and period
  • periods per org unit, first and last
  • org units with a gap in a covariate
  • org units missing from the locations file
uv run chap-test-data time-checks datasets/21-facilities-20k-weekly-10y datasets/23-org-units-100k-weekly-10y

It uses DuckDB to measure; which engine Chap will use is not decided. --memory-limit caps DuckDB's memory (default 1 GB); above it, DuckDB spills to disk.

On a 12-core MacBook (2026-11-26):

Rows All checks Peak memory 10.4 million (20,000 facilities, 10 years weekly) 0.2 s about 0.9 GB 52.2 million (100,000 org units, 10 years weekly) 3.7 s about 1.6 GB

Nearly all the time goes to the duplicate check. Even the largest dataset is checked well within a DHIS2 route's timeout.

docs.title: Comparing with JSON
docs.text: Today the Modeling App sends a dataset to Chap's make-dataset endpoint as JSON. This page compares that with the Parquet upload, on the same data.

docs.title: On one machine
docs.text:
compare uploads each dataset three ways to the same Chap: as Parquet, as make-dataset JSON with providedDataColumns (what the Modeling App sends today), and as make-dataset JSON with providedData (one object per value, the older form). The JSON bodies carry the same settings and locations as the Parquet files.

uv run chap-test-data compare 02-district-weekly 03-facility-points --dry-run --repeat 3
uv run chap-test-data compare 03-facility-points --dhis2 --dry-run --format parquet --format json-columns
uv run chap-test-data compare 03-facility-points --wait        # real import, with the worker's time

Dry runs directly to Chap, median of 3, on 2026-11-26:

Dataset Format Body Request 1,500 facilities x 365 weeks Parquet 3.8 MB 0.98 s JSON columns 31.4 MB (8.2x) 1.37 s (1.4x) JSON rows 211.5 MB (55x) 15.18 s (15.5x) 2,000 facilities x 365 weeks Parquet 5.1 MB 1.30 s JSON columns 41.9 MB (8.2x) 1.87 s (1.4x) JSON rows 282.0 MB (55x) 20.66 s (15.9x) 1,500 areas, 2,048 points per border Parquet 40.8 MB 10.57 s JSON columns 158.1 MB (3.9x) 13.00 s (1.2x) JSON rows 338.2 MB (8.3x) 26.14 s (2.5x) 150 districts x 365 weeks Parquet 1.2 MB 0.43 s JSON columns 6.3 MB (5.1x) 0.40 s (0.9x) JSON rows 24.3 MB (20x) 1.92 s (4.4x)
  • Size: at facility scale Parquet is about 8x smaller than today's JSON. How much depends on the data: smoother test data gave 14x, so real data may land in between. With large polygons the geometry dominates and the gap narrows to about 4x.
  • Server time: Parquet is 1.2x to 1.4x faster. For small datasets the two are about even.
  • Worker: the background import takes the same time for every format, because all three queue the same job (54 s at 1,500 facilities).

docs.title: Over a real network
docs.text:
On one machine sending costs almost nothing. In production the upload crosses a real network, from the user's browser to DHIS2 and on to Chap, and there the size of the body counts.

slow-link.sh measures that. It runs the curl upload in a small container on Chap's Docker network whose network interface is shaped with Linux tc netem: real delay on every round trip and a capped rate, so TCP behaves as it does on a slow, distant link.

./slow-link.sh --delay 100ms --rate 10mbit --dry-run datasets/03-facility-points
./slow-link.sh --delay 100ms --rate 10mbit --dry-run --json datasets/03-facility-points
./slow-link.sh --delay 300ms --rate 2mbit --dhis2 --dry-run datasets/03-facility-points

03-facility-points (1,500 facilities x 365 weeks), a dry run through a DHIS2 2.43 route, on 2026-11-26:

Link Parquet (3.8 MB) Today's JSON (31.4 MB) JSON takes Same machine 1.1 s 1.4 s 1.2x as long 50 Mbit/s, 20 ms delay 1.9 s 6.7 s 3.6x 20 Mbit/s, 50 ms delay 3.1 s 14.7 s 4.8x 10 Mbit/s, 100 ms delay 5.0 s 28.1 s 5.6x 2 Mbit/s, 300 ms delay 18.9 s 134.1 s 7.1x

Straight to Chap, without DHIS2, the times are within 0.1 s of these.

  • The slower the link, the closer the gain gets to the size difference. On a fast link Chap's own work dominates; on a slow one sending does, and Parquet sends 8x fewer bytes.
  • The upload is the slow direction. Many links upload far slower than they download, and a dataset goes up.
  • JSON cannot be compressed on the way. Browsers do not compress request bodies, and DHIS2 routes strip gzip, so the 8x difference stays 8x on the wire.
  • The DHIS2 route sends Parquet files twice to Chap until DHIS2-22596 is fixed. That leg is usually between servers, so it costs little: about 0.1 s here.
  • The route's timeout starts after the upload, so a slow upload does not time out, but the user waits for every byte.

chap-test-data upload and compare also take --bandwidth (Mbit/s), which only paces the sending, without delay. It needs no Docker but leaves out what latency does to TCP.

docs.title: The common datasets
docs.text:
./generate-datasets.sh                  # all, including the large ones: a few minutes and a few GB
./generate-datasets.sh --standard-only  # the 16 standard ones only: seconds

They are written to datasets/ with a fixed seed (42), so they are the same on every machine. Each is written as Parquet, as GeoJSON locations (locations.geojson) and as the JSON body the Modeling App sends today (make-dataset.columns.json). The datasets Chap must refuse are written as Parquet only.

docs.title: Standard
docs.text:
They use 4 value columns: disease_cases, population, rainfall and mean_temperature.

Dataset Size Expected answer 01-small-monthly 10 districts x 36 months 10 imported 02-district-weekly 150 districts x 365 weeks 150 imported 03-facility-points 1,500 facilities x 365 weeks 1,500 imported 04-facility-polygons 1,500 areas x 365 weeks, 2,048 points per border 1,500 imported 05-facility-points-2000 2,000 facilities x 365 weeks 2,000 imported 06-geojson-locations 50 districts x 104 weeks, locations only as GeoJSON 50 imported 07-masked-ranges 20 x 36 months, cases masked 201801 to 201803 by the metadata 20 imported 08-no-metadata 10 x 24 months, no chap.* keys; the name comes from the file name 10 imported 09-covariate-gaps 20 org units, 3 miss one covariate value 17 imported, 3 rejected 10-missing-locations 20 org units, 4 missing from the locations file 16 imported, 4 rejected 11-bad-duplicate-rows one row twice 422 12-bad-text-column a text column in the observations 422 13-bad-no-time-period no time_period column 422 14-bad-spec-version chap.spec_version 2 422 15-bad-not-parquet a CSV file named observations.parquet 422 16-named-columns 20 x 36 months, columns malaria_cases, population, precipitation, temperature_2m 20 imported

docs.title: Large
docs.text:
10 years with all 10 value columns. Only the first fits Chap's Phase 1 upload (1 million rows, 100 MB per file); the others are the size stored files (Phase 2) are designed for.

Dataset Rows Phase 1 answer 20-phase1-max-weekly-10y 1,900 x 522 weeks = 991,800 1,900 imported 21-facilities-20k-weekly-10y 20,000 x 522 = 10.4 million 413, file too large 22-org-units-100k-monthly-10y 100,000 x 120 = 12 million 413, file too large 23-org-units-100k-weekly-10y 100,000 x 522 = 52.2 million 413, file too large

23 gets no JSON body: it would be about 5 GB.

docs.title: Your own
docs.text:
Every dataset is one command, so a variation is one command too:

uv run chap-test-data generate my-test --org-units 5000 --years 5 --period monthly
uv run chap-test-data generate districts --org-units 300 --geometry polygon --format geojson
uv run chap-test-data generate malaria --column malaria_cases --column population --column precipitation
uv run chap-test-data generate gaps --org-units 50 --covariate-gaps 5 --drop-locations 2
uv run chap-test-data generate --help
Options What they set --org-units, --years or --periods, --period weekly or monthly, --start-year The size --columns N The first N of disease_cases, population, rainfall, mean_temperature, min_temperature, max_temperature, relative_humidity, soil_moisture, ndvi, elevation (default 10) --column NAME (repeatable) Your own column names instead; the first is the target --missing The share of missing target values (default 0.002) --geometry point or polygon, --corners N Facility points (default) or district areas with N points per border (default 800) --format with csv, geojson, json-columns or json-rows (repeatable) Other formats besides Parquet --masked START:END, --no-metadata, --spec-version The settings in the file's metadata --covariate-gaps N, --drop-locations N Org units Chap must reject --duplicate-rows N, --text-column NAME, --drop-time-period, --not-parquet Files Chap must refuse --seed N The same files every time; without it the seed is random and recorded in expected.json

The observations are written in batches of org units, so memory stays small: 52 million rows take about 25 s and 650 MB. The other formats are converted from the Parquet files in batches too.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text: --format Files (always) observations.parquet, locations.parquet geojson locations.geojson csv observations.csv (time_period, location, then the values) and locations.geojson json-columns make-dataset.columns.json: the make-dataset body with providedDataColumns, as the Modeling App sends today json-rows make-dataset.rows.json: the older body, one object per value

docs.title: The values
docs.text:
Values follow chapkit's TestDataGenerator, so models tested with either tool see the same ranges:

Column Values population 50,000 to 1.5 million, fixed per org unit rainfall 150 +/- 130 mm per period, following each org unit's own season mean_temperature 24 +/- 7 °C on a regional cycle; min and max 4 to 8 °C below and above disease_cases a per-org-unit level that follows the season, plus 0.06 x rainfall other covariates seasonal, between 0 and 100

The schema is Chap's, not chapkit's: periods as Chap stores them (2016W01, 201601, with real ISO weeks, so some years have a week 53) and DHIS2-style org unit ids.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
• Districts (--geometry polygon) tile a country-like map near Nairobi: no gaps, no overlaps, and jagged borders shared by both neighbours. A border has about 800 points by default, the median of chap-core's example boundaries, and is about 1.7 times as long as a circle of the same area, as real borders are (1.4 to 1.9 in those files).
  • Facilities (--geometry point) cluster around a few towns in each district, always inside it, and the parent column names that district: one per 50 facilities.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
You need uv and Python 3.13 (uv installs it for you).

git clone https://github.com/dhis2-chap/chap-test-data && cd chap-test-data
uv sync
uv run chap-test-data --help

Generating datasets needs nothing else. Uploading needs a running Chap, and the DHIS2 route a running DHIS2; both run in Docker.

docs.title: Start Chap
docs.text:
The Parquet upload is on the chap-core branch feat/dataset-parquet-upload:

cd ../chap-core
git switch feat/dataset-parquet-upload
docker compose -p chap-test-data up -d --build
curl localhost:8000/health

The project name chap-test-data keeps this stack and its volumes apart from any other Chap you run. Chap answers on http://localhost:8000, without a token unless CHAP_API_TOKEN is set in chap-core's .env.

docs.title: Start DHIS2 (for the route)
docs.text:
dhis2/ holds a DHIS2 that joins Chap's Docker network, and a script that creates the route chap pointing at Chap. The first start takes a minute or two.

cd dhis2
docker compose up -d          # DHIS2 2.43.2.1
./setup-route.sh              # waits for DHIS2, then creates the route chap -> http://chap:8000/**
cd ..

Another DHIS2 version: DHIS2_TAG=2.42.7.1 docker compose up -d, after docker compose down -v so the database starts fresh. For a DHIS2 elsewhere, set the connection settings below and make sure it allows the route's target in route.remote_servers_allowed.

docs.title: Connection settings
docs.text:
Every command that talks to Chap takes these as options or environment variables:

Variable Default CHAP_URL http://localhost:8000 CHAP_API_TOKEN none DHIS2_URL http://localhost:8080 DHIS2_USER, DHIS2_PASSWORD admin, district ROUTE_CODE chap

docs.title: Stop
docs.text:
cd dhis2 && docker compose down -v && cd ..
cd ../chap-core && docker compose -p chap-test-data down -v

docs.title: Developing
docs.text: make lint runs ruff, mypy and pyright, the same tools as chap-core. make test runs the tests, which need no running Chap. make docs builds this site, and make build the package. CI runs them on every push.

docs.title: Uploading and checking
docs.text: Start Chap first (see Getting started).

docs.title: One dataset
docs.text:
uv run chap-test-data upload --dry-run datasets/03-facility-points   # validate only
uv run chap-test-data upload --wait datasets/03-facility-points      # import, and wait for the job

docs.title: Every dataset against its expected answer
docs.text:
uv run chap-test-data check                    # every folder in datasets/
uv run chap-test-data check --dhis2            # the same through the DHIS2 route

check dry-runs each dataset and compares Chap's answer with the folder's expected.json: how many org units it imports and rejects, or which error it gives.

docs.title: Through a DHIS2 route
docs.text: --dhis2 sends the upload to DHIS2's route API, which forwards it to Chap, as the Modeling App does. DHIS2 2.42.3 and later forward each file twice (DHIS2-22596); Chap ignores the extra copies, so the result is the same as without DHIS2. Tested on DHIS2 2.41.11, 2.42.7.1 and 2.43.2.1.

docs.title: With curl
docs.text:
The same, without Python:

./upload.sh --dry-run datasets/03-facility-points
./upload.sh --dry-run --json datasets/03-facility-points     # the make-dataset JSON body instead
./upload.sh --dhis2 --dry-run datasets/03-facility-points
./check-all.sh                                               # every dataset against expected.json

curl -X POST "http://localhost:8000/v1/crud/datasets/files?dryRun=true" \
  -F observations=@datasets/03-facility-points/observations.parquet \
  -F locations=@datasets/03-facility-points/locations.parquet

curl -u admin:district -X POST \
  "http://localhost:8080/api/routes/chap/run/v1/crud/datasets/files?dryRun=true" \
  -F observations=@datasets/03-facility-points/observations.parquet \
  -F locations=@datasets/03-facility-points/locations.parquet

With a token, add -H "Authorization: Bearer ..." to curl, or set CHAP_API_TOKEN.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Measured on a MacBook with Docker Desktop, chap-core feat/dataset-parquet-upload:

  • Every dataset gave the expected answer, directly and through DHIS2 routes on 2.41.11, 2.42.7.1 and 2.43.2.1, and a real import of 03-facility-points succeeded through each.
  • Real imports took 4 to 6 s for the request at 1,500 to 2,000 facilities, and about 20 s with large polygons, where checking the geometry takes most of the time. The worker then stores the data in the background: 54 s at 1,500 facilities, 70 s at 2,000.
  • The DHIS2 route's timeout (30 s in the Modeling App, 60 s at most) counts from the end of the upload, so a slow upload does not use it up.
